Since Fraternities have arisen to that dignity and
prominence that insures their permanence, it is in
cumbent upon every member and every Chapter to
endeas^or to keep alive the fraternal feeling and to
draw inter-Fraternity lines closer. Now the influence
of a
Fraternity extends beyond the atmosphere of the
Chapter and College, and is recognized in the world.
This is more noticeable every year. The Fraternity is
no longer merely the object for the enthusiasm of
boys in College, but is a body to whom venerable
men^�
Divines, Authors, Judges, Governors, Senators
and Presidents �
delight to show their devotion.
The great problem of Fraternities once was,
"
How
shall the organization be continued and insured against
death?" Chapter Houses, strong graduate associa
tions and reciprocal labor have solved that question.
Now the pronounced aim of a good Fraternity is
elevation of tone, not perpetuation �
that is settled
beyond dispute �
but perpetuation with the best
results.
Upon the younger graduates must devolve the duty
and task of producing in the Fraternity that unity of
feeling and interest which persuades the older mem
bers that they are as
truly members of Psi Upsilon as
when they surrounded the Chapter altar. The desire
of graduates to keep up their Fraternity affiliation is
shown in their presence at conventions and in their
interest in their own Chapter Houses.
With the conviction that our prosperity is to a great
extent measured by the interest of our Alumni, let
every Psi U. man, when he leaves his College, have
the well-defined purpose of stimulating the Fraternity
spirit of those whose many years of business cares
have given little time for the renewal of old associa
tions. To the accomplishment of this purpose Gradu
ate Organizations are the most effectual aids.
By this time nearly all our chapters have held their
initiations, and the Fraternity has within her fold a
large number of new men�
new in college and new in
Psi Upsilon. It is an
important period in the life of
the men, and the time for the exercise of an important
duty by the Fraternity�
that of educating the new
members.
One of the chief requisites of a valuable member
is an intimate knowledge of the characteristics, history
and policies of the Fraternity. An early acquaintance
with these details determines the position and useful
ness of a member. Generally a new initiate measures
the Fraternity by a chapter standard, without any idea
of the complex relations of the Fraternity at large.
A complete knowledge of the concerns of the society
is necessary for the intelligent exercise of the rights
and privileges of an active member of a
Chapter. It
is not possible to consider any important Fraternity
question in its full scope without the information which
results from a study of the facts upon which our poli
cies are based.
If in addition to the experience of the upper classes,
the lower ones have a familiarity with Fraternity usages,
the dignity and position of the Chapter will be greatly
elevated. The drill imposed upon younger members
by certain Chapters is certainly commendable and
should be adopted by all.

THE PROCEEDINGS OF THE SEMICEN
TENNIAL CONVENTION.
The public exercises of the Semi-Centennial Con
vention will be published in book form, with heavy
paper cover and on
antique paper. The typographi
cal appearance will be made especially attractive.
The original plan at the time of the convention was
to pubUsh the proceedings in The Diamond, but sub
sequent consideration has convinced us that the record
of an event so notable and important as our Fiftieth
Anniversary should be preserved in distinct and sepa
rate form. There is hardly a live member of Psi
Upsilon who would not desire to possess a book so
valuable, not only on account of its Fraternity charac
ter, but on account of its literary worth.
It will contain the Introductory Address by Hon.
Alexander H. Rice, the Oration by Hon. Joseph R.
Hawley, the Essay by Charles Dudley Warner, the
Poem by Prof Hjaltrar H. Boyesen, the Ode by Prof.
Calvin S. Harrington, the Address of Welcome to the
Delegates by Prof. I. B. Price, the speeches at the
Banquet by Hon. Hooper C. Van Vorst, President of
the Banquet, Hon. Joseph R. Hawley, Hon. Alexan
der H. Rice, Hon. Sterling G. Hadley, Hon. John M.
Wheeler, Dr. Maunsell Van Rensselaer, Prof. Goldwin
Smith, Hon. Samuel W. Jackson, Benj. H. Bayliss,
Hon. D. Ward Northrup, Charles Dudley Warner,
Hon. Ehsha Taylor, Rev. George D. Baker, D.D.,
Hon. Albion W. Tourgee, Robert Lenox Belknap,
Prof. Hjalmar H. Boyesen, Prof Edward H. Williams,
Jr., Herbert L. Bridgman and Frederick G. Fincke.
An account of the Reception, the list of Delegates
and members in attendance, a chart of the Banquet
Table, and such other incidents as
may be of interest,
will be given.

will form a
frontispiece.

REMINISCENCES OF THE STUDENT LIFE
OF CHARLES DUDLEY WARNER.
In the judgment of the intelligent reader of to-day,
the writings of Charles Dudley Warner entitle him to
a conspicuous place among men of letters. Few are
unacquainted with his history in later hfe, and the
result of his labors, published in that series of works
which have so captivated the reading public. Sketches
of his hterary career, and criticisms of his books, have
appeared so often that a general knowledge of them
cannot but have become familiar. It is as a student,
perhaps, that Warner is least known. Reminiscences
are vain, except as they give us a glance behind the
veil, and instruct us in the hidden past, when some
now noted name
represented the personahty of only a
college boy. So we
present this article, of reminis
cences
mainly, taken catch-as-catch-can from the lips
and letters of old friends, trusting it may prove of
interest.
In the case of Charles Dudley Warner, the college
boy was father to the man. He entered college in
1848 from the bookish quietude of Cazenovia, with a
native passion for belles lettres studies, and his three
years in college kept him reasonably busy with what
ever intellectual venture was welcome and inspiring.
As a
general student he stood fairly. He had no
special liking for the treadmill round of undergraduate
work; and if he let his mathematics alone very
severely, it was with a tacit understanding that he was
to be let alone quite as
severely by the mathematical
professor.
He is recalled as a
blender, smooth-faced lad, no
ticeable chiefly for the great mass of brown hair tumbhng over his forehead, and the big eyes that seemed
to be especially prominent. During junior year his

THE DIAMOND. 15
place in the chapel was beside one of the pillars that
support the old-fashioned high gallery. To one of
the chapel-goers of to-day that pillar is still haunted
by the clinging adumbrations of a straight, lithe stu
dent with a far-away look in his great blue eyes as the
Sunday sermon dragged its tedious length along. He
had a trick in conversation of looking at a
person
long and steadfastly when he was interested, as though
he saw through and beyond that one out into some
vague realm where he alone had access. He had a
mobile face that reflected and intensified the thought
'
that was within him ; and when that set, far-away ex
pression came into his eyes, it was worth while to be
silent and to listen.
He was rather shy and distant in his manner, or to
put it more properly, he was delicate and refined, and
shrank instinctively from whatever was coarse and
vulgar. Everybody liked him, and yet he had few in
timates. In general he was reserved and self-con
tained, though companionable and wholly unselfish ;
but to those who found their way into his real heart he
was open as the day, frank, demonstrative, and on
occasion even enthusiastic in his affection. To say
that he was the most popular man in his class means
much, because he was so indifferent to the popular
arts.
He could easily drop off into a limitless brown
study whenever the drill of the class-room grew dull
and wearisome. In his chosen way he was always in
dustrious and enterprising. Writing for prizes began
during his junior year, and his name stands with that
of Dr. D. J. Pratt, of Albany, at the head of the long
double line of Hamilton graduates who have been
laureled for English essays.
In his literary exercises he was easily at the head.
Ordinarily the composition of a college boy is not a
thing that fills either gods or men with delight ; but
when he rose to read, all ears were eager to listen. It
is said that sometimes even the Professor, in his awful
"
bear-box," was seen to unbend from his stately dig
nity and give the nod of approval. His contributions
to our little chapter paper were always characteristic.
The odd, quaint way of putting things ; the genial,
kindly humor ; the bright wit, that the reading world
so weir knows and appreciates now, were all there.
To a friend, Mr. Warner once said that the character
istics of his style were partly shaped by his habit of
writing letters to correspondents of either sex, whose
friendship kept him under willing bonds to do his best.
His graduating oration on
"
Great Words
"
was in his
own racy style, and altogether different from the con
ventional spread of
"
something to speak well." The
brilliant success in literature of the man is no surprise
to those who knew the boy. It needed no prophet to
predict his future.
He was a
great reader, fairly omnivorous, and old
traditions declare that no book in the college library�
not so large then as at present
�
escaped him. He
flung himself into a book all over with a kind of furious
delight, that none but he who has felt it knows. At
that age a book is a book. Poetry, essays, history,
criticism, plays, novels�
everything must give up its
literary wealth to the boy burning with an insatiable
thirst for reading. An old friend relates that to see
him of a summer afternoon, curled up in the broad
window-seat of his room, poring over a book, was to
see one wrapt beyond all care or thought of what was
around him. He lived and moved and had his being
in books.
In a wholesome way, Charles Dudley Warner was
fond of the woods and of lonely rambles where the
pulse of nature could be heard to beat. A lady who
had something to do with his three meals a day, reportsthat when he came into a late supper he was apt to
bring a handsome apology in the shape of a string of
trout from the Kirkland woods. That trout stream is
not so well stocked now as it was thirty years ago, but
it still crosses the highway near the southern line of
the John Kirkland farm, and a local artist has put on
canvas a section of it that passes for
"
Warner's Trout
Brook."
Perhaps not even the stirring success of his after
life has given him more real satisfaction and pleasure
than did those college days. It may be doubted if he
enjoys more heartily any of the grand receptions
tendered him by society than he did the old-time
Wednesday evening whist parties with Lester, and
Townsend, and Pope at the corners of the table, and
with the well-browned tobacco pipes and the old
broken-nosed yellow pitcher of harmless egg-nogg for
refreshment. Nor can he have ceased to remember
the occasional meetings of the "Turkey Club," with
pink-faced old Terry sneaking up the back stairs,
bringing the nicely cooked gobbler in a covered
basket, to be carved with a pen-knife, and washed
down with the overflowings of a bucket of surrepti
tious cider from old Smith's cider press back
"
on the
hill."
He is now the busy editor of a
great daily paper ;
and the name of Charles Dudley Warner is known
and his books are admired over both continents.
Probably few of his classmates had eyes to foresee the

1 6 THE
glory that now invests his name. Yet they could not
help loving him for his lovable gifts, and now they all
rejoice, if living, in his world-wide success as a de
scriptive and humorous writer. And possibly even
yet he looks back with pleasant thoughts to the days
when he was only
"
Charley

among the boys at
Hamilton, thirty odd years ago.
E. M. Barber, Psi, '84.
THE INFANCY OF THE SECRET SOCIETY
SYSTEM.
Over half a
century has elapsed since the now wide
extended secret society system sprang into existence
at Union College. Looking back over the intervening
years, it is a study of profit and curiosity to review the
causes which led to the establishing of these fraternal
bands, and to notice the ups and downs of their succeed
ing careers. At the expiration of the first quarter of the
century, Phi Beta Kappa, the venerable corner stone
of modern secret societies, had lost its character of
secrecy, retaining its honorary organization, into whose
precincts men were admitted in appreciation of their
standing in College. On the other hand, two
flourishing literary societies, with large membership
rolls and a
degree of secrecy; furnished a
binding
chain for general association, but lacked the connect
ing link of individual friendship. With the tokens of
mystery which had traditionally surrounded the pre
vious existence of Phi Beta Kappa and the literary
societies as models for improvement, there arose a
desire to organize a
friendly union which should com
bine warm
friendship and sociability as its selecting
principles, and which would possess an air of impressiveness necessary to perpetuate its existence. In
1825 several seniors of the class of 1826, endeavoring
to combine these principles, formed the Kappa Alpha
society, pledging undying friendship and mutual assist
ance. If premeditated or not, this sworn
fealty was
attended by many exhibitions of its sincerity, and soon
the name of secret society became a bar to general
association. Nevertheless, the organization thrived,
and candidates, attracted by the secrecy and influence
connected therewith, were ever
ready to be initiated
into the terrible mysteries.
Exclusiveness in the course of time became the order
of things�
a condition of affairs most undesirable to
other men who considered themselves equally worthy
the friendship which those bands afforded. Rivalry pro
duced opposing organizations, and the succeeding year,
1827, gave birth to Sigma Phi and Delta Phi. In these
Kappa Alpha found worthy foes ; and amid the conflict
incident with an early existence, it is interesting to
recognize the origin of many of the established customs
of later-day Fraternities. To distinguish themselves
from rival bodies, and to characterize their particular
organizations, badges of peculiar design were worn.
Kappa Alpha selected a square key to be used as a chain
pendant ; Sigma Phi chose a
monogram design, the
Sigma placed over the Phi, while Delta Phi took the
Maltese cross, with the letters Delta and Phi placed
upon a center oval. All of these pins bore symbolic
designs, and were calculated greatly to impress the un
initiated. No societies possessed lodge rooms
in those days, but meetings were held regularly in the
different members' rooms, and frequently in one of the
public taverns of Schenectady�
in the latter cases,
the meetings being supplemented by interesting
spreads. Notwithstanding the opposition of burlesque
organizations and College authorities, these germs of a
future greatness grew and flourished. In 1831 Sigma
Phi introduced the now generally practiced plan of
placing branches in neighboring collegiate institutions,
and at Hamilton chartered a sister organization known
as the "Alpha Chapter." Kappa Alpha, failing in a
similar attempt at Hamilton, gave a charge to some
Williams College applicants. About this time, the
fourth in this series of notable societies founded at
Union sprang into existence. Four members of the
class of 1836 and three of the class of 1837 organized
themselves in the fall of 1833 into a society known as
the Psi Upsilon. They chose as a badge a diamondshaped design bearing upon it clasped hands, having
above the letter Psi and beneath the Upsilon.
Many-persons, in giving causes for the formation of the
four societies which I have mentioned as founded at
Union prior to 1834, have claimed that they had their
origin in factions created for the control of elections in
the Philomathean and Adelphic hterary societies. The
records of these societies show that none of the
founders of Sigma Phi or Delta Phi were members of
either literary organization at the time of the forma
tion of these secret unions. Likewise of the names
of the seven founders of Psi Upsilon, not one is
found on the membership rolls of either the Philoma
thean or
Adelphic society. This, certainly, disposes of
the claim of their origin for political purposes, and
there is every reason to beheve that they were designed
for mutual, social and literary benefits. The years
between the establishing of Kappa Alpha and Psi
Upsilon witnessed the birth of several minor organiza
tions. Some came into existence for the mere pur-

THE DIAMOND. 17
pose of burlesquing the bona fide organizations.
They sported' grotesque badges, followed peculiar cus
toms, and were, in every respect, intended to discoun
tenance the existence of the supposed evil. Their
existence, however, was necessarily short-lived. From
the time of the appearance of Kappa Alpha there had
existed a smouldering opposition to secret societies,
and with the advent of Psi Upsilon this took form.
In the spring of 1834, two associations were formed,
whose avowed purpose was the extinction of secret
societies. They took the names of the Fraternal So
ciety and Equitable Union. Their membership at the
time of formation was large, and at subsequent periods
numbered as high as one hundred each. Finding
that the principles of the secret societies were beyond
their reach, they abandoned their undertaking. The
Fraternal Society after a
precarious existence, under
the garb of semi-neutrahty for a
period of twenty-five
years, was merged into a
chapter of Alpha Delta Phi.
The Anti-Secret Confederation, as the Equitable Union
was afterwards called, entered the ranks of Delta
Upsilon Chapters in 1861.
In November, 1839, the neutral opposition gained
control of the Philomathean Society, and the follow
ing amendment was made to the Constitution of the
society :
"
No member of a secret society shall ever
become a member of this society ; and if any one here
after becoming a member of this society shall join any
secret society, he shall be expelled from this society
on conviction of the same." At one of the last
meetings of the Philomathean Society in June,
1 84 1, several of the prominent members of that
body appeared, wearing a new badge in token of
their connection with a society known as Chi Psi.
This action was in open violation df the amend
ment adopted in November, 1839, and at the
meeting of the Censors' Council, on July 3, 1841,
Secretary Taber (a Chi Psi) was instructed to sum,rnon
before that body Messrs. Brush, Major, Spencer,
Duane and Berthond, July 8th, to stand trial for
violation of the Constitution. The Secretary's min
utes of July are headed "A fight ! A fight ! M^ke a
ring !
"
The closing paragraph reads :
"
An attempt
was made to proceed to business of a character more
suitable than that which was ultimately effected,
which it behooves the Secretary to leave unrecorded
as entirely unworthy of the sedate character of this
body. Adjourned in confusion." The minutes of the
society meeting of a later date show that the amend
ment forbidding secret society members to join the
Philomathean was repealed. These men whose names
I have mentioned, together with three others, were
the founders of Chi Psi. This society had a long and
successful career at Union, but getting low in members,
its charter was withdrawn in 1877, apparently, as the
Chapter was on the threshold of a new lease of life.
The year 1847 brought forth the last of the famous
six societies created at Union. At that time Union
College was at the height of its prosperity, 299 names
being on its roUs. The Sophomore class numbered 72,
and out of this, six members combining, formed the
Theta Delta Chi Society. They selected a shieldshaped badge, bearing the letters Theta Delta Chi
Ijeneath crossed spears and above two stars. Their
life ended at Union when the war of the rebellion and
the losses at the South drew so many from the College
rolls. In the year 1859, 440 names were on the rolls
of Union College, and in that year nine secret socie
ties were contestants for positions at Union, namely ;
A. K. E. and Z. W. The first six, whose courses I
have traced, have become powerful Fraternities, having
co-existent branches in a score of collegiate institu
tions, and four now exist at Union �
Chi Psi and
Theta Delta Chi having disappeared from the roll.
With the spread of these organizations in other Col
leges, we note the origin of many other Fraternities.
The latter, witnessing the existence of these branches,
created kindred organizations. Some of these have
remained local in their existence, while others have
branched out and grown into powerful Fraternities.
Dr. Nott, the famous president and educator, opposed
these bodies, but after some had complied with his
request to exhibit their Constitutions, he lent his aid
to their advancement, and during fifty years' experi
ence often made the remark, now traditional, that he
easily governed the College by the open recognition
and sagacious use of these clubs.
The worth and usefulness of these organizations is
everywhere admitted, and their value frequently
attested by members eminent in theological, pohtical, literary and professional pursuits. Numerous
graduates have manifested an attachment to their
Alma Mater, which was often greatly due to the warm
friendship formed in the fraternal circle. Anfong
Union's prominent graduates and firm supporters, are
fouiid the names of many of the founders and early
workers in the creation of this secret society system.
Kappa Alpha's list furnishes: Preston King, Ward
Hunt, Prof. Joy and Augustus Schell. Sigma Phi:
Hon. John Cochrane, John Bigelow, Major-Gen.
Townsend, ex-Gov. Hoffman and ex-Gov. Hamtranft.

Delta Phi: Hon. George F. Seward, Rev. William
Wilson and Hon. H. S. Randall. Psi Upsilon : Presi
dent Van Rensselaer, of Hobart, Hon. Clarkson N.
Potter, ex-Gov. Rice, Bishop Littlejohn, Hon. Fred
erick Seward, President Arthur and Judge Van Vorst.
Chi Psi :
Major-Gen. Duane, Hon. Robert Earl, MajorGen. Albert L. Lee and Commodore Meredith. Theta

FROM A FOUNDER.
When the form of the original badge of the Psi
Upsilon was adopted in 1833, it could not have been
foreseen that, in after years, it would give a name to
the Society's publication. It seems, however, that
some one saw how appropriately The Dm.mond might
represent the Society, and in a certain sense be the
Society, since all the Chapters are in it with their inter
esting reports of work accomplished. Thus it will be
seen how the few thoughts presented originated.
A kind and thoughtful relative and friend sent me
the photographic picture of the brethren present at
the semi-centennial as they are seated upon the steps
of the Capitol at Albany. I see but few familiar faces,
but know that men are there who are
filling, and will
in the future occupy, many of the highest offices in
Church and State, and I am filled with admiration.
>^ It was a small beginning in 1833, and the material
/ out of which Psi Upsilon was created seemed rather
/ crude, coarse and common�
a half dozen young men
V in some of the lower classes, mostly from country
places �
diffident, unpohshed, unattractive, just intro
duced to College life. Who could have expected
anything permanent, valuable, brilhant, from such
material ? But there are mysterious forces silently at
work, and grand results often come from small, un
promising beginnings ; the coarse carbon becomes
the. Dianiondj the Psi Upsilon of '33~Fecomiiig the
Diamond of '83.
It isvaliiable in its influence and brilliant in its
record. Young men as
College students must have
society of some kind, and, as a rule, find little, if any,
in the cities where our largest Colleges are
located; so
that it becomes a
necessity, in order to the proper
cultivation of their social nature and their moral
characters, that they may be drawn closely together
socially with those of their own kind. I think I can
say, as one of the founders of the Psi Upsilon, that it
originated in such a
necessity ;. for though in those
days we had as noble a President and corps of Pro
fessors as any College can boast of, yet there was no
fellowship with students, and they repelled rather than
attracted.
It was my good fortune, some three years ago, to
spend a most enjoyable evening with the brethren of
Columbia College in their Chapter rooms, and I was
most forcibly impressed with the value of the Society
to College students. The young men present seemed
drawn together in bonds of the closest fellowship, and
I could well understand that the attractions of their
surroundings and employments were more potent for
the cultivation of the mind, the morals and the social
quality, than the guilded outside allurements tending
to their demoralization and ruin.
In conclusion, I need hardly refer to the brilliancy
of the record of Psi Upsilon. As in the past and pres
ent, so doubtless it will be in future. When another
half century shall be finished, our young men of
to-day win see inscribed on the roll of membership a
longer Ust of honorable names than in the past half
century.
I think I see in my photographic picture young men
from our different Colleges and Universities rising up in
scores to take the front seats soon to be vacated by
our venerable fathers and founders. Let the \
Diamond shine and sparkle in all its briUiancy and V
beauty, and may the day be distant when it shall fail /
to attract the young men of our Colleges. /
Rev. Samuel Goodale.

RESULTS OF CONVENTION.
One of the most valuable outcomes of the conven
tion held in Albany is the increased and increasing
sympathy between the different chapters. Not that
the charge of apathy could ever be laid in justice
before any Chapter's door, but that the warm feeling
and friendly interest which have always characterized
us have received a fresh impetus. Acquaintance with
and conversation between representative men from
various Chapters serve to make known and disseminate
all the different plans and methods for promoting
active chapter hfe far more efficiently than correspon
dence, though that will always occupy its own peculiar
sphere of usefulness. It is among chapters as among
brothers in the individual Chapters, intercourse and
the exchange of ideas, face to face, are the most
potent means of advancement.
No former convention, probably, ever afforded such

THE DIAMOND. 19
opportunities for intercourse between the various ele
ments that go to make up the great body of our Fra
ternity. From founders down to the most recently
initiated brother, every grade of experience was repre
sented, and, inspired by the prevailing ideal of celebra
tion and good fellowship, each delegate seized every
chance to meet and greet every other one, and to
gether to rejoice and grow enthusiastic. Such conver
sations, laden as they were with heartiest feeling, were
bearers of many of the triviaUties and commonplaces
of Chapter procedure and economy that would never
suggest themselves to the letter writer and that are
emphatically characteristic. These little ideas, carried
like seed and transplanted into the different soils of
other chapters, often take firm root and grow to be
come valuable principles. In the remembrances of
minor incidents of conversation, in the interchange of
opinions, in the meeting and mingling of true friends,
in the thousand and one ways in which man meets
and mingles in man, in all that results from compan
ionship in men pursuing the journey of life along the
same road, the Chapters have been especially benefited
by this convention.
In view of this increased interest a thought suggests
itself from a few of Professor Goldwin Smith's remarks
at the banquet, wherein he spoke of the excellent par
liamentary procedure which marked the business
sessions of the convention and which he held to be
equal in every respect to the sessions of ParUament or
of any other deliberative body that he had attended.
Preparation for active parts in deliberative bodies is

Buffalo claims as citizens a goodly number of the

vented by sickness or other engagements from carrying

Under the nom de plume of Paul Siegvolk, author of

Walter Ashwood," we take pleasure in recognizing
Mr. Albert Mathews B '42, author of
"
A Bundle of
Papers."
The work is written in a clear and racy style, concise
without being studied, critical without being captious.
The topics chosen are of interest to the scholar or to
the man of business who chooses to have an hour of
quiet thought. Indeed the work may be said to
appeal particularly to the latter, for it treats of many
of those subjects with which he has a
partial acquain
tance in his every day life, viz. :

He is a

"Musings of a
City Railroad Conductor."
"
My Friend Bosworth Field
"
is a
charming paper
that will delight any one who has been within cohege
walls ; for it will call up familiar, if not altogether
pleasant, scenes in the life of anyone who has ever
been a bold sophomore or a luckless freshman.
Throughout the '.' Bundle of Papers
"
there is abund
ant evidence of the bright mind that has closely
observed the different phases of life and drawn there
from lessons whose worth will be appreciated by those
who value moral and social excellence as
applied to
the actions of men. A cultivated man can wish for
no more genial, entertaining and instructive compan
ion than this charming volume that tells pleasant tales,

templation. "A Bundle of Papers" should find a

The Freedom of Faith. By the Rev. Theodore T. Munger, D. D.
Boston: Houghton, Mifflin & Co.
Rev. Theodore T. Munger, B '51, so well known
through his valuable work
"
On the Threshold," and
through his sermons, now gives to the world another
harvest of thoughtful years,
"
The Freedom of Faith."
It is an attack upon the growing materialistic ten
dency of the present as well as upon the bigotry and
fanaticism of the past. The "
New Theology
"
he
proves to be perfecdy compatible with the teachings
of the Bible read aright.
Unlike many of the men whose minds are
engaged
upon similar fields of thoughts, he uses logic and
reason, not for their own sake, but as guides to truth,
nor does his divine reverence aflow him once to
forget the supremacy and rulership of God.
Mr. Munger discusses the Bible in its solidarity and
not in the light of single passages. His line of thought
is bold and original, and will be very effective in
checking infidelity, which grows from strained, preju
diced and unnatural interpretations of the Scriptures.
He has raised religion out of the trammels of stern,
unchangeable systems and showed its adaptability to
humanity.
He accepts the theory of physical evolution as the
probable method of physical creation, and as having
an analogy in morals ; but he accepts it under the fact
of a
personal God who is revealing himself, and of
human freedom, facts not to be ascertained in the
limits of a material philosophy. He harmonizes reli
gion and science, and still maintains the sovereignty
of God.
"
The Freedom of Faith
"
is one of the most com
prehensive, able and conclusive expositions of the new
theology that has yet been written.
